analysis.one_liner: Reinstates the oil and chemical excise taxes that fund Superfund toxic site cleanups, with help for businesses forced to relocate.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in May 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill brings back the expired Superfund excise taxes that make oil and chemical companies pay into the fund that cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites, raising the per-barrel rate and updating it for inflation. It also adds tar sands and oil shale oil to the taxed definition of crude oil, and it helps small businesses and residents who live or work on or near Superfund sites with a $10,000 moving deduction and Small Business Administration loans. The bill never moved past its initial committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near Superfund sites gain because cleanup money would again come from a tax on polluters instead of being borrowed from general tax revenue. Small businesses forced to relocate from a Superfund site could deduct up to $10,000 of moving costs and qualify for SBA disaster and economic injury loans, and homeowners whose primary residence sits on or next to a Superfund site could qualify for relocation loans. Communities gain from faster cleanups of contaminated sites.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, raising it from 9.7 cents to 15.8 cents per barrel, with automatic inflation adjustments so the rate does not erode over time.
Reinstates the per-ton excise taxes on feedstock chemicals (such as benzene, ethylene, and mercury) that historically funded Superfund cleanups, also adjusted for inflation.
Expands the excise-tax definition of crude oil to include tar sands and oil shale derived oil, so those producers pay into the fund like conventional oil producers.

Lets small businesses deduct up to $10,000 of costs of relocating a business on or near a site on (or proposed for) the national priorities list, while barring companies that are themselves potentially liable for the site's contamination from using the deduction.

Directs the SBA to run a pilot program of five-year direct relocation loans for small businesses and individuals whose principal place of business or residence is on or adjacent to a Superfund site, and allows economic injury loans for affected small businesses, with $10 million authorized for fiscal years 2020 through 2024.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners and petrochemical and chemical manufacturers pay the reinstated excise taxes. Some of that cost would be passed through to consumers in the form of slightly higher fuel and chemical product prices. Federal taxpayers fund the SBA loan program, though at a modest $10 million authorization.

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on oil and feedstock chemicals are typically passed at least partly into fuel and product prices, so consumers would bear some of the tax through higher costs.

The small business relief is narrow: the relocation deduction is capped at $10,000 and the SBA loan program is authorized at only $10 million over five years, small amounts relative to relocation costs and the number of businesses near the more than a thousand sites on the national priorities list.
A new tax on oil production raises energy costs at the margin, an objection its opponents would raise, particularly for tar sands and oil shale oil newly covered by the tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is favorable to the public: since the polluter-paid Superfund taxes lapsed in 1995, cleanup of toxic sites has been paid from general tax revenue, so this bill shifts that burden back onto the oil and chemical industries whose products created the sites, with modest pass-through to consumers. The small business provisions are genuine but small. The bill's main weakness is not its design but its fate: it never received any committee action, so none of its provisions took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means and Small Business Committees after referral and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on May 21, 2019, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Small Business Committee.
The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referrals; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action was ever taken.
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and chemical companies are better off because the bill died: they continued to pay no Superfund excise tax, and the cost of cleaning up the nation's worst toxic sites stayed with general taxpayers. Small businesses and residents on or near Superfund sites got no relocation relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; general taxpayers

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and submitted it to the House.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill to a committee vote after it was referred to his committee.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never reached a vote, so no record shows how opponents would have voted.

industries.note: The bill reinstates a 15.8-cent-per-barrel Superfund tax on their products and broadens the taxable definition of crude oil to include tar sands and oil shale output. Since the tax lapsed in 1995, cleanup costs these levies once covered have fallen on general taxpayers.
Reinstates per-ton excise taxes on dozens of feedstock chemicals (benzene, ethylene, mercury, and others) that fund Superfund cleanups, ending a quarter century in which they paid none.

industries.industry: Small businesses located on or near Superfund sites
industries.note: Would get a $10,000 relocation deduction and access to SBA disaster and economic injury loans, plus a new five-year relocation loan pilot. Businesses liable for the contamination are excluded.
